title: Preface
summary: They say if you work in one industry long enough, you become part of the wiring. I guess that’s me.
content:
They say if you work in one industry long enough, you become part of the wiring. I guess that’s me. For more than twenty years, I’ve lived and breathed telecom, not just the polished tools and technologies, but the guts of it. The chaos, the midnight escalations, the improbable comebacks, and the quiet victories nobody ever posts about.

So let’s get one thing straight: this isn’t a textbook. It’s my story of navigating the whole messy ecosystem, the networks, the people, and my life. My career was never a straight line. It was more like a signal that bent, roamed, dropped, reconnected, and somehow, always found its way forward.

I wrote this for the people who build things from behind the scenes. The thinkers. The firefighters. The leaders who play the long game. It’s full of the moments that made me, not all of them glorious, but every single one of them real. Because leadership isn’t always loud, growth is rarely pretty, and sometimes, the best stories are buried deep in the code.

Let’s decode them together.

— C. C. Khaw

title: The Starting Line
summary: Every legend has an origin story. Mine started with a terrible internet connection.
content:
Every legend has an origin story. Mine started with a terrible internet connection.

There was no grand strategy. No spotlight. Just the demonic screech of a 56k modem in a cramped little workspace near Hotel Istana in Kuala Lumpur. It was 2001. I was just a kid fresh from college, a technical support executive at Computer Protocol (M) Sdn Bhd, running on a lean diet of cheap coffee and raw curiosity. My job? To support customers scattered across the globe, Myanmar, New Zealand, India; who were staring at a broken system. My tools? A phone, an email client, and a remote-control program that moved with the speed of melting ice. Symantec pcAnywhere. Yeah, that’s the one.

It wasn't glamorous. But it was honest-to-God real.

## The Soundtrack of My Youth

We didn’t have a "cloud." We had a server rack that hummed with the heat of a small sun. Forget Zoom. We had eye-wateringly expensive long-distance calls that chewed through the company’s phone bill and my social life.

The customers on the other end didn't care that I was young or still figuring things out. They just wanted to know one thing: "Can you fix it?"

And I always said yes. Always. Even when a voice in my head was screaming, *How? You have no idea what you're doing.* That blind, reckless optimism? It was my only superpower.

## Road Warrior in Training

The strange part is, I wasn’t just stuck behind a screen. They sent me everywhere. I was flown out to Myanmar to fix VoIP systems for the military government. I found myself in Singapore, Indonesia, and New Zealand, hauling a laptop that felt heavier than my luggage and trying to install networks while fighting off jet lag with terrible hotel coffee.

Every stamp in my passport taught me something. Myanmar taught me patience. Indonesia, how to improvise. Singapore, precision. And New Zealand? It taught me that sometimes you have to go to the other side of the world to get a clear view of yourself.

## Lessons in the Trenches

The emergencies were constant. A customer's system down at midnight; another unable to make calls during the World Cup. It all felt like life or death. I spent nights working until the sun came up, resetting routers with what felt like nothing more than sheer willpower.

But the systems always came back online. And slowly, so did my confidence. I wasn’t just solving problems anymore. I was becoming the kind of person who runs towards them.

In two years, I’d gone from the new support guy to a trainer, an installer, and the resident VoIP wizard. I was demoing solutions at trade shows in Dubai and running training for new hires. It was a crash course in how technology works, how people break it, and how to fix both without breaking yourself.

## Building Something I Couldn't See

I see it clearly now, but back then, I had no idea I was building a foundation. Every late-night incident was a lesson in persistence. Every frustrated customer, a masterclass in empathy. Every airport, a lesson in humility. I didn't have a mentor. I had a dial-up modem. And it was enough.

My whole philosophy started to form right there. Technology isn't about the servers or the code. It’s about the person on the other end, desperately hoping it all works. That’s why I stayed up. It's why I crawled under desks. It's why I double-checked every line of config before deployment. Because I cared. Deeply. Especially when no one was watching.

## Graduation Day

By late 2003, it was time to move on. Not because I was bored, but because I had learned everything I could. I needed a bigger stage. A tougher challenge. Maybe even better coffee. I didn't know what was next, but I knew I was walking away with more than just tech skills. I was taking a work ethic, an adaptability, and a quiet confidence that whatever came next, I’d figure it out. Because I had before.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *The clearest signal in any new role isn’t in your job description; it’s in your customer’s frustration. In your first 90 days, don’t just learn the product, learn the pain it’s meant to solve. Run towards the toughest support tickets. Volunteer to talk to the angriest client. The empathy you build and the ownership you demonstrate when no one is watching will become the foundation of your career. This is your first, best chance to prove you care more about their problem than your comfort.*

title: Debugging My Way Up
summary: If my first job taught me how to swim, my time at ADC Software Systems and LogicaCMG taught me how to survive the storm.
content:
## The Grind That Built My Spine (2003–2007)

If my first job taught me how to swim, my time at ADC Software Systems and LogicaCMG taught me how to survive the storm.

This was my welcome to the 24/7 grind. I was a Senior Support Engineer in a global team, which is a fancy way of saying I had a shift roster that spanned over weekends. I was part of a 25-person rotation, troubleshooting in real-time, half-asleep but always sharp. I didn't just take calls anymore. I started taking ownership. I stopped asking for permission to lead. I just did.

## The Mental Gym

Every ticket was a new workout. One hour, you’re helping Maxis Malaysia optimize their broadband network; the next, you’re on the phone at 3 a.m. with a panicked client whose system just crashed. No excuses. Just a problem with your name on it.

I got better over time and I stopped thinking about my list of tasks and started focusing on the impact I could make. I didn't just fix what was broken; I dug in and figured out why it broke. I started rebuilding workflows and sharing what I learned. I was turning chaos into clarity because, well, somebody had to. And that somebody became me.

## Leading Without a Title

It started small. Answering a question for a junior teammate. Taking the lead on a critical incident because I already knew the system inside and out. Before I knew it, I wasn't just "on shift." I was leading the shift. It was never official. No one gave me a new title. But people started coming to me first. The seniors. Even the managers. They knew I wouldn't panic. I wouldn't pass the buck. I wouldn't drop the ball.

## The Three Words That Mattered Most: "I'll Handle It."

There was a night when a US customer had a massive outage. The team was exhausted. You could feel the collective groan when the ticket landed. No one wanted it. I looked at the screen, took a breath, grabbed another coffee, and heard myself say the three words that would become my brand: "I'll handle it."

Those words changed everything. They taught me to step into the fire when it’s uncomfortable. To take the heat, even when it’s unfair. To find a solution, even if I had to learn how on the fly. They taught me real accountability.

## LogicaCMG: The Major Leagues

By late 2004, I was ready for a bigger stage. I jumped to LogicaCMG, one of the giants of telco infrastructure. This was not just a support role anymore; this was the big leagues. LogicaCMG's platforms were the engine behind messaging and prepaid services for almost every major player in Asia-Pacific: Celcom, Indosat, SingTel, Sun Cellular, Telstra, Optus. My job was simple: keep those engines running. No matter what. The pressure was immense. Millions of subscribers depended on the systems I was now responsible for.

## The Unsung Heroics

Ever enjoy a Xpax prepaid "Length of Stay" bonus on Celcom? I helped deploy that. MMS pre-delivery charging for SingTel? That was me. Migrating Intelligent Service Node clusters for FarEasTone in Taiwan, or running migration for Vodafone New Zealand? Me again.

There were no press releases. No big announcements. Just the quiet satisfaction of knowing my work was powering millions of connections across Asia. I wasn’t on the billboard. I was in the network's bloodstream.

For three straight years, my performance rating was "Exceeds Expectations." Not because I was chasing a score, but because I refused to let things fail. I was the guy who could fix a bug, calm down a client, and mentor a junior engineer all before lunch. Why? Because I gave a damn. It’s that simple.

## The Purpose in the Pain

My perspective shifted. This wasn't a grind anymore; it was a craft. Underneath all the brutal hours and the constant pressure, I realized something profound. In this business, you don't just keep the lights on. You keep people connected. That felt sacred. I found meaning in the messy backend. Purpose in every text message that got delivered on time.

## Moving On

By 2007, I knew I had hit a ceiling. I could have stayed and been comfortable, but I wanted a new kind of challenge. I wanted to evolve. So I made another move, this time to a deep technical role at Accuris Networks. Leaving wasn’t easy. That team was like family. But I walked away with something far more valuable than comfort: a confidence forged in fire. The support trenches taught me to stand up when everyone else wants to sit down. That lesson alone made every sleepless night worth it.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Stop waiting for permission to lead. Leadership isn't a title that’s given; it’s influence that’s earned through action. The next time your team faces a problem no one wants, be the first to say, “I’ll handle it.” This isn’t about being a hero; it’s about being accountable. Shifting your mindset from completing tasks to owning outcomes is the single fastest way to build trust and become the person your team and your leaders turn to when the pressure is on.*

title: Roaming Rebels
content:
**Deploying Dreams Across Borders (2007–2009)**

In 2007, I completely switched tracks. I left the structured world of telco support for something wilder. I joined Accuris Networks, an Irish startup with a rebellious mission: to make different mobile network standards talk to each other when they weren't supposed to. We wanted to make Wi-Fi behave like cellular and bend stubborn standards into flexible human experiences. It was pure, beautiful madness, and I was all in.

They brought me on as a Senior Engineer, but titles were mostly meaningless there. What mattered was whether you could make sense of a log file screaming in hexadecimal while your flight was boarding in ninety minutes. My job was to help telcos do things they had been told were impossible. I was ready.

And then, I met Kent Choong, but more on him later.

## From the Engine Room to the Cockpit

My desk was still in Kuala Lumpur, but the problems I solved spanned oceans. Clients from New Zealand to Poland all had the same question: "Can we roam where we're not supposed to?"

My job was to say "yes," and then figure out how to make it true. There was no manual. No SOP. Just protocol traces, coffee, and a healthy dose of creative insanity.

I wasn't following a playbook. I was writing it.

## Jet Lag and Joy

That era turned me into a traveling technician. I was constantly on the move, from Telecom NZ to Alltel USA, CITIC 1616 in Hong Kong, and Sferia in Poland. Every deployment was a new puzzle, a new country, and another hard drive jammed into my carry-on. Some trips were glamorous. Others? Not so much.

I once worked in a data center in Hong Kong so cold my fingers went numb. But I loved every minute of it. There was a unique rush in making technology talk across different standards, in turning isolated networks from islands into bridges.

## Inter-Technology Magic

What we were doing felt almost illegal at the time :-) Roaming from a CDMA to a GSM network? That was science fiction to most telcos. They called it IIF (Inter-technology Inter-working Functions).

This is where we were pulling off integration miracles, enabling full GPRS data roaming between networks that were never designed to speak to each other. We weren’t just engineers. We were rebels with lab coats. And I was living the dream, solving real-world problems with packets and passion, not PowerPoints.

## No Titles, Just Impact

My business card said "Senior Engineer." But my real job title changed by the hour: presales, support, trainer, negotiator. I ran Proof-of-Concepts, pitched new ideas to executives, and handled escalations when a roaming hub went sideways. I worked side-by-side with developers, debugging Diameter logs and designing SIM testing scripts. Why? Because in a small team with a massive vision, that’s what impact looks like. You learn the most when there’s no one shielding you from the storm.

## Philosophy at 30,000 Feet

I remember being on a red-eye flight somewhere over the Pacific, sleep-deprived and buzzing with ideas, when I wrote this in a notebook: "Technology only matters if it shrinks the world. If it brings a voice from Wellington to Warsaw, if it lets a parent call home across oceans, then the late nights are worth it."

That became my personal mission statement. Every integration wasn't just a technical win; it was a human one. We weren't just enabling roaming. We were rewiring relationships.

## Small Wins, Big Stories

I’ll never forget the moment we got our first inter-technology roam live for Telecom NZ. Everyone was braced for it to fail. To be honest, even we had our doubts. But it worked. Cleanly. The first successful handshake between networks that were never meant to see eye-to-eye.

There was no applause. Just the quiet hum of packets flying and a customer on the other end whispering, "Thanks." That whisper echoed louder than any standing ovation ever could.

## The Lessons That Stuck

That chapter taught me that the smallest teams can do the boldest things. It taught me that if you know your protocols and trust your gut, even the impossible starts to look manageable. And it taught me that airports aren't just waypoints; they’re places to reflect, reframe, and recharge. Above all, it taught me that you don’t need a cape to be a hero in this business. Just a laptop, a plan, and a stubborn belief that you can fix anything.

## The Fire Was Lit

By mid-2009, I was a different person. Sharper. Hungrier. I’d earned scars from systems that fought back and had stories that would never fit on a resume. I was ready for the next leap, to climb up the stack, not just roam within it. And so, I made my move back to LogicaCMG (Acision), but this time, I wasn't there to fix things. I was there to architect them.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Identify the biggest, most stubborn constraint in your industry, the thing everyone says is “impossible.” That is where your opportunity lies. To foster a rebel mindset in your team, reframe the question from “Can we do this?” to “What would it take to make this possible?”*
>
> *Find the human purpose behind your technical work, shrinking the world, connecting a parent to their child and use that story to fuel the persistence needed to write your own playbook.*

title: Architects of Connection
summary: They say the best architects don’t just design; they see the stories in the systems. By 2009, I was done just installing gear or troubleshooting links.
content:
## From Tech to Strategy (2009–2012)

They say the best architects don’t just design; they see the stories in the systems. By 2009, I was done just installing gear or troubleshooting links. I had stepped into a pre-sales and solution architect role at Acision.

My job was no longer to answer questions, but to anticipate them. I was learning to speak the language of both business and technology. It was less about logs and more about logic. Less "which wire goes where," and more, "how does this platform make you money?"

## From Cables to Concepts

I’d walk into boardrooms where the sales people wore sharp blazers and the customers wore skeptical expressions.

"Can this really be done?" they'd ask. I’d nod slowly. "It can. Let me show you how."

Then I’d hit the whiteboard like my life depended on it, layering protocols, timelines, and dependencies into diagrams that danced. The real product wasn’t the platform. It was confidence. And I sold it with clarity.

My job wasn't to sell the dream; it was to make the dream believable.

## From Solving to Selling

Every solution I designed had two simple goals: It had to work, and it had to win the deal.

That meant juggling client meetings in Jakarta on Monday, then catching a flight to Manila by Wednesday for a live bid. It meant understanding what the customer really wanted, not just what they said they wanted.

Sometimes they wanted scale. Other times, they just wanted reassurance. I learned to speak both languages fluently.

## Herding Tigers

My role also involved working with a team of solution architects and presales engineers across APAC. We weren’t a formal team; we were a band of tinkerers and troubleshooters trying to craft regional value propositions that made strategic sense. And Asia is a beast. The Philippines wanted agility. Singapore wanted compliance. Indonesia just wanted the best price. My job was to balance it all and still leave room for innovation. A good architect doesn’t copy-paste. They custom-build, with precision, empathy, and a whole lot of caffeine.

## How to Win a War Room

There’s a special kind of energy in a bid war room. The deadline is breathing down your neck. Product managers are arguing about feature readiness. Sales leads are trying to shave down the price. And me? I’d be in the corner, reworking the architecture, removing bottlenecks, and squeezing every last drop of performance out of our servers. I loved it. Not despite the pressure, but because of it. That’s where I thrived, where the stakes were high and performance was king.

## Philosophy in Layers

I learned something crucial during this era: technology doesn't just have layers; it teaches in layers. The Network Layer taught me humility, latency doesn’t lie.

The Application Layer taught me flexibility, no two clients are the same.

The Business Layer taught me diplomacy, not every trade-off is technical.

And the User Layer taught me humanity, people just want things that work.

The better I got at reading that full stack, from systems to financials, the more I became a trusted advisor.

## The Soft Skills

My most important skills weren't writing JIRA epic or drawing architecture diagrams in Visio. They were listening to a client ramble just to hear their real pain point. They were rephrasing system limitations without killing the mood in the room. They were guiding a junior engineer through their first bid with grace. People call them soft skills. They're not soft. They’re the code that keeps the whole system human.

## Pivoting to Discipline

By early 2011, I felt that familiar itch. I had outgrown the whiteboards and wanted more business depth. Just like that, a door opened at Openet, an Irish BSS/OSS powerhouse looking for someone who could wear both the technical and strategic hats. It was time to move.

After the creative chaos of Acision, Openet felt like a high-stakes chess match. It wasn't about wild new ideas; it was about mastering structure, navigating long sales cycles, and dealing with the legacy systems that are the beating heart of every telco. I came in as a Regional Technical Sales Manager, and it was clear from day one this wasn't a role for the faint of heart. It demanded technical precision, commercial sharpness, and a good dose of diplomacy.

## The Sales Cycle Ballet

The rhythm was intense. Respond to an RFP in the Philippines. Demo a new policy manager to a customer in Jakarta. Catch a red-eye to Colombo for a workshop. Then a midnight call with the Dublin HQ. Some days I was designing architecture on a boardroom whiteboard; other days, I was translating complex workflows into simple benefits for a procurement team. I was the bridge between innovation and implementation.

## People Buy People

We were often competing against tech giants with deep-rooted contracts. But our wins were meaningful because they were earned through trust and persistence. Customers didn't just buy our software; they bought our conviction. One of the most underrated skills I learned was how to influence without making a lot of noise. You don’t need to dazzle with jargon. You just need to listen, synthesize, and speak in a way that makes people nod.

My time at Openet was only a one-year chapter, but it left a permanent mark. I learned how to navigate telecom sales with maturity. I learned how to lead without formal authority. And I added a new dimension to my experience: the discipline of structured growth. It was something that would serve me again and again. With that, I stepped into the next phase, one foot in business, the other in tech, with the map of APAC in my briefcase.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Practice becoming a translator. Take a complex technical feature your team is working on and explain its value to a non-technical stakeholder (like a marketer or a salesperson) in three simple sentences.*
>
> *The real product you’re selling is confidence, and confidence is delivered through clarity. Learn to listen for the unstated need behind a customer’s request; are they asking for a feature, or are they asking for reassurance? The ability to architect trust is more valuable than the ability to architect code.*

title: Wi-Fi and Wild Ideas
summary: In 2012, I walked back through the doors of Accuris Networks. But I wasn't the same guy.
content:
## Building the Accuris Business in APAC (2012–2016)

In 2012, I walked back through the doors of Accuris Networks. But I wasn't the same guy. I wasn’t there to play the riffs; I was there to write the album. I wasn’t there to tinker. I was there to build a business. They gave me a blank canvas with the title: Director, Business Development, APAC. I got to work from ground zero.

## Basecamp: Kuala Lumpur. Battlefield: All of Asia.

My office was a base in KL with a laptop, a suitcase, and an airline rewards program that quickly became my best friend. APAC wasn't just a region; it was a collection of moods. Every market had its own rhythm. Malaysia was conservative but loyal. Vietnam was chaotic brilliance. Indonesia was potential wrapped in latency. Australia demanded polish. Thailand smiled while negotiating you into the ground. My job was to find a way to land Wi-Fi monetization deals in all of them. Every flight was a gamble. Every handshake was a pitch. Every "maybe" was a win in disguise.

## Selling the Future

We weren’t just pushing products; we were pioneering new tech like Wi-Fi offload and SIM-based authentication on Wi-Fi networks. Most operators stared at us like we were trying to sell them a UFO. "Wi-Fi... for seamless mobile roaming?" they'd ask. "Login-less? Like magic?"

"Yes," I'd say. "Like magic. Only powered by protocols and sleep deprivation :-)"

I had to become an evangelist. I walked into boardrooms from Sydney to Taipei, preaching the gospel of seamless connectivity. And when their own networks inevitably dropped during my presentation, I’d just smile and say, “Exactly. This is why you need us.”

## The Breakthroughs

In 2012, we landed Maxis Malaysia as our first Wi-Fi offload customer. That was huge. It gave us credibility, cash flow, and a massive dose of confidence. A year later, we pulled off a moonshot by signing China Mobile International to deploy the world’s first WRIX-based Wi-Fi Roaming Hub. It still sounds cool, right? Then in 2014, we delivered Accuris’ largest-ever Wi-Fi platform to Telekom Malaysia. We’d made it. Those deals weren't just wins; they were validation that our crazy ideas weren't so crazy after all.

## Building a Team That Could Fly Without Me

The thing I'm still proudest of from that era? The zero turnover rate on my team. I scaled our APAC presence by 500%, not by throwing money at people, but by treating them like they mattered more than the metrics. I gave them ownership. I gave them room to fail. I tried to be the kind of leader I wish I would have when I was in my 20s. You don’t keep great people by chaining them to a desk. You keep them by making sure they know they’re building something meaningful with you.

## The Conference Grind

I became a fixture at every telecom conference in the region. Booths, panels, demos, I did it all. Sometimes I was in a suit. Other times, I was holding a buggy demo unit, just praying it wouldn’t crash mid-presentation. Either way, I showed up. And clients noticed. The brand grew. My inbox exploded. My calendar basically died. But the deals kept flowing.

## A Philosophical Upgrade

These years matured me. I wasn’t just chasing revenue; I was crafting regional strategy. I was learning how different markets leapfrog infrastructure, how regulation shapes innovation, and how spectrum isn't just bandwidth, it's power. Telco isn't just about telecom. It's about trust, timing, and translation. It's about taking the painfully complex landscape and making it feel simple.

## The Crossroads

By 2016, I had done what I came back to do. We had doubled our customer base and expanded across APAC. I had hired and mentored an all-star team. I could have stayed, played it safe. But something in me was getting restless again. I felt a call for a new kind of challenge. And right on cue, Sandvine came knocking. When growth shows up at your door, you don’t ask, "Why me?" You ask, "What’s next?"

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *When pioneering a new product or idea, your first task is evangelism. Find your first "lighthouse" customer, the one who believes in your vision and over-deliver for them. Their success story will become the proof that silences skeptics. To build a loyal, high-performing team that can achieve this, delegate outcomes, not tasks. Give your people a mission and the ownership to achieve it, and they will build something with you, not just for you.*

title: The Architect in the Shadows
summary: Before the big product launches and the headlines, there was a man quietly crafting perfection in the background. That man was Kent Choong.
content:
## The Story of Kent Choong

Before the big product launches and the headlines, there was a man quietly crafting perfection in the background. That man was Kent Choong. Code sculptor, logic whisperer, and my co-pilot through some of the wildest chapters of my career.

## The First Encounter

I met Kent at Accuris Networks, that Guinness-fueled Irish startup trying to stitch Wi-Fi and cellular into something that actually worked. I was the Senior Engineer flying around with a toolkit of test SIMs; Kent was the Software Engineer, though that title felt like a massive understatement.

He didn't make a big entrance. He just opened XML configs like they were poetry and patched Diameter bugs with surgical precision. I’ll never forget our first real test: a customer escalation in Hong Kong. It was late. Roaming SIMs had gone rogue. While everyone else was panicking, Kent plugged in his laptop and said, "Give me five minutes." Four minutes and one sip of coffee later, the customer was back online.

I remember thinking, *Who is this guy? And why isn’t he running the place?*

## Code, Connection, and a Kinship

What started as a work relationship quickly became something more. We weren't just engineers; we were tinkerers, thinkers, and tired dads trying to juggle toddlers and TCP/IP. Our lives began to overlap in uncanny ways. Our kids were in the same kindergarten. Our houses were just a few hundred meters apart. Our mums literally traded veggie prices at the morning market while we were fueled by caffeine, hammering out a 130-page tender submission.

What are the odds? Kent became my confidante, my co-conspirator, and the one person I could trust with both a crazy idea and my hotel room key.

## Around the World in Packets and Memories

We didn’t just work together; we flew across time zones like caffeinated falcons. Each trip left a memory.

**Dubai** – The iPhone 6 has just launched. We had a long layover. So what did we do? We bolted from the airport at 4 a.m., jumped in a cab, and raced through the neon-lit streets to snag the latest iPhones before anyone else. We barely made it back for our flight, but the feeling of clutching that new tech? Worth it.

**Brunei** – The only "entertainment" outlet open late was a Coffee Bean & Tea Leaf. That’s where we were, sipping lattes and dissecting deployment logs when the email landed. Bhutan wanted a Wi-Fi offload demo. It was our next mission. We just looked at each other, laughed, and said, "Let's go."

**Bhutan** – The land of Gross National Happiness. But even happiness needs better bandwidth. The local telco was choking on 3G congestion. We flew in, landed at Paro, still one of the most mind-blowing airport landings in the world and pitched how we could offload their traffic to Wi-Fi. It wasn't just a demo; it was diplomacy, showing how tech could support even the most remote corners of the globe.

**Dublin** – Our second home. The Accuris HQ. We’d work all day, drink Guinness all night, and walk the cobbled streets of Temple Bar, laughing about how the same bug had followed us all the way from Malaysia. Dublin became our lab, our tavern, and our classroom, all at once.

## From Builder to Founder

In 2016, Kent did something bold, something not enough brilliant engineers do. He became a founder. He started his own company, brewing new Wi-Fi technology and building smarter connectivity for the region. The first three years were brutal. Late nights, lean resources, and the relentless pressure of being the CTO, CFO, CEO, and janitor all at once. But Kent pushed through. The momentum built. Soon, flagship projects rolled in, proof that his vision wasn't just valid; it was valuable. The guy who used to quietly fix bugs at midnight? He was now shaping the future of connectivity on his own terms.

## The Essence of Kent

What makes Kent so special? He doesn't care about applause. He leads without volume and delivers without drama. He’d rather ship a clean build than give a keynote. But when you really sit down with him, you see the depth of thought and the quiet conviction he carries. In a world of loud pitch decks and tech-bro egos, Kent is the opposite. Subtle. Steady. Brilliant.

## Why This Chapter Exists

This book might have my name on the cover, but some of its best chapters, the most complex deployments, the wildest memories, all have Kent’s fingerprints on them. He was my partner in crime, my dev room confidant, my go-to dinner buddy in cities that don't sleep. My brother.

You don’t build a legacy alone. You build it alongside people like Kent Choong. And for that, I’m forever grateful.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *You don't build a legacy alone. Look around your organization and identify your "Kent", the quiet expert, the reliable partner, the person whose skills perfectly complement yours. This is your most important professional relationship. Invest in it. Celebrate their successes publicly. Grab coffee or a beer and talk about life, not just work. The trust forged in these informal moments is the resilient connective tissue that will get you through the toughest projects.*

title: Sales, Strategy, and Switches
summary: By 2016, I was ready to trade my Wi-Fi cape for a different kind of challenge. That's when Sandvine came calling.
content:
## Jumping Between Giants (2016–2019)

By 2016, I was ready to trade my Wi-Fi cape for a different kind of challenge. That's when Sandvine came calling. If Accuris was about making connections, Sandvine was about controlling them. They were the traffic cops of the internet. I came on as a Regional Sales Engineer for ASEAN, tasked with bringing clarity to the chaos of digital traffic. It was part technical, part political, and part philosophical. I loved it.

## Welcome to the Layer 7 Jungle

At Sandvine, the stakes were sky-high. We were helping telcos understand and monetize every single bit flowing through their pipes. You’d be amazed at the drama hiding inside a gigabyte of data. "Why is Netflix lagging?" "Can we block torrents without causing a riot?" The answers were buried deep in packet inspections and bandwidth shaping. In this game, truth is measured in throughput. And trust? In uptime.

## The Region That Never Sleeps

My playground was ASEAN, and it never played by the rules. Vietnam wanted to prioritize gaming traffic. Myanmar telecom market was just opening up, wanted everything for free. Thailand wanted YouTube, but not too much. Singapore wanted it clean, clear, and compliant. It was like solving ten Rubik’s Cubes at once, blindfolded, on a moving tuk-tuk. And yet, I found my rhythm.

There’s something oddly beautiful about a live trial in a client’s network operations center. Wires everywhere, everyone watching, and you, calm and collected, knowing it’ll work. Until it doesn’t. Then you smile, crack a joke, reroute some configs, and make it work anyway. That was my secret weapon: resilience wrapped in humor. I didn't just bring demos; I brought confidence on demand.

## The Bid Battles

The bids at Sandvine weren't just about price; they were mini-wars. You had to outmaneuver Cisco's glossy presentations, out-charm Huawei's discounts, and out-think local players who had been friends with the CIO since 2004. I didn't win every deal, but I won the ones that mattered. Because I learned to listen deeper and speak simpler. I could dance between network engineers and C-level executives without missing a beat.

## A Quick Detour: The Ruckus Rebellion

Mid-2017, I made a quick detour to Ruckus Networks as a Regional Sales Director. The mission was to grow their portfolio in the Service Provider space across Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Myanmar, Brunei, and Cambodia. It was a big sandbox. It was fast, furious, and I got to work with everyone from mobile operators to cloud players, stitching together B2B deals from scratch. The best part? Building long-term partnerships that were personal, not just transactional. You’re not just selling Wi-Fi access points. You’re promising stability in an unstable world.

## The Human Connection

Jakarta in the rain, Ho Chi Minh in the dust. These places were more than business trips; they were reminders that connectivity is a lifeline, not a luxury. In those moments, pitching a solution felt like preaching a sermon. And when a deal landed, I didn't just celebrate a commission; I celebrated the possibility it created.

## The Lesson

Those years taught me that selling tech isn't about features; it's about faith. That culture is the protocol underneath every handshake. And whether you're shaping packets or partnerships, the magic is in the details. I grew sharper, but also softer. The more systems I shaped, the more I realized that tech is never the end. It’s the means. People are always the point.

By 2018, I felt a shift coming. A whisper that said, "You’ve played the wide field. It's time to go deep again. Time to build." And right on cue, Fortesys came knocking, offering me a blank canvas to paint a whole new strategy. Next chapter, next challenge. Same Khaw, just a little wiser.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *In a crowded market, you win by out-listening, not out-shouting. The next time you’re in a competitive bid, spend 80% of your energy diagnosing the client’s true pain point and 20% pitching your solution. Practice the art of the simple explanation; it’s a sign of confidence, not a lack of depth. Remember that culture is the protocol beneath every handshake. If a deal feels off, analyze the human signals you might be missing.*

title: Layovers, Launches, and Lessons
summary: They say travel broadens the mind. In telecom, it also tests your resilience, your caffeine tolerance, and your airport-navigation skills.
content:
## Tales from the Telco Road (2007–2016)

They say travel broadens the mind. In telecom, it also tests your resilience, your caffeine tolerance, and your airport-navigation skills. For years, I practically lived out of a suitcase. I knew airport lounges better than my own living room. My passport had more stamps than a collector's album. And somewhere along the way, airport terminals turned into classrooms and boardrooms became battlegrounds. These weren't just business trips; they were the chapters that shaped my career. Each destination had its own lesson, its own flavor, its own scar. They formed the connective tissue between my technical skills and my human leadership. Here are ten stories from the road that left a mark.

## @ 1: Solo Across Seven Skies

**KL → Dublin → Little Rock → DFW → LAX → TPE → KL**

In 2008, I took on one of the most intense assignments of my career: a solo journey that spanned 18 days, 7 airports, and more than 30,000 kilometers. It was a whirlwind mission with nothing but a laptop and a drive to make some CDMA magic happen.

The assignment was to deploy our Activation HLR solution for Alltel USA. But first, a critical pitstop in Dublin, our global headquarters. Flying into Dublin was about absorbing every last byte of knowledge from the core engineering team. I met with architects and QA engineers, reviewed scripts, and collected the "deployment package", a sacred bundle of configs, cheat sheets, and SIM cards. The sessions were intense, fueled by fish and chips and Irish stouts.

Then came the real ride: Dublin to Little Rock, Arkansas. When I landed, I was welcomed by frost. It was cold, quiet, and very Southern. But the Alltel team was sharp, collaborative, and curious. They wanted results. And I was the guy holding the playbook.

For nearly a week, I worked out of a nondescript office building, debugging signaling issues and configuring remote interconnects. My evenings were spent alone in a hotel room with log files and weak coffee. No Kent on this trip. Just me and the problem.

Once the deployment was live, I booked the long flight home: Little Rock → DFW → LAX → Taipei → KL. I remember sitting in the lounge at DFW, reflecting on what I had just pulled off. It wasn't the most elegant deployment, but it worked. There was no applause. Just a quiet, personal victory. When I finally landed back in KL, jetlagged and dazed, my teammates could barely believe the route I’d taken.

That trip taught me ownership, resilience, and how to navigate ambiguity, both in airports and in architecture. I wasn’t just a deployment engineer on that trip. I was the whole show. And in many ways, that’s where I truly learned to fly.

## @ 2: Pints in Kilkenny

You haven’t really bonded with your sales team until you’ve done it over pints of Kilkenny… in Kilkenny. It was the end of a brutal sales quarter at Accuris, and the global team was in Ireland for a week of workshops. To break the intensity, our VP of Sales declared we were heading out of Dublin for the weekend. Destination: Kilkenny, a medieval city with charm, beer, and 400-year-old cottages that might have been haunted.

No PowerPoints. No customer escalations. Just a team of sleep-deprived sales and tech folks finding their way to the local pub. In Kilkenny, titles dissolved. The VP became the guy who couldn’t find his boot. The sales engineer became the bartender. And I became the unofficial grill master at a midnight barbecue.

Amid the fun and storytelling, something else happened. We started to understand each other as humans. As parents, spouses, and karaoke disasters. It was a rare window into the people behind the metrics, and it changed how we worked together. There were no performance reviews in that cottage, just moments of shared humanity. And those moments translated into smoother launches and quicker trust. I still have the photo, slightly blurry and definitely joyous, all of us holding up pints as if we’d just landed a billion-dollar deal. We hadn't. But the culture we were building that weekend? Worth far more.

## @ 3: The Johnny Fox’s Madness

There's something poetic about kicking off a sales strategy in a city where the wind can slap the optimism out of your face. Welcome to Dublin in January. It was Sales Kick-off Season, that sacred time of buzzwords and budget battles. At Accuris, this wasn't just a meeting; it was a ritual. Three days of marathon sessions, mapping out APAC rollouts and debating Wi-Fi offload tactics.

But when the sun dipped, the real magic started. We headed to Johnny Fox’s Pub, "Ireland’s highest pub," nestled in the Dublin mountains. Our team piled into a shuttle bus, buzzing with caffeine and adrenaline. What followed was legendary. A fire-roasted dinner, a live Irish folk band, and a surprise dinner show that involved step dancing. Deals were toasted. Failures were turned into jokes. Promises were made, not just to hit targets, but to have each other’s backs.

Around midnight, I found myself outside in the freezing dark, standing beside the VP of Engineering. He asked, “You think we’ll pull off that China Mobile thing?” I replied, “Only if you code while I sell.” He grinned. "Deal."

Strategy is important, but alignment often comes from laughter, not spreadsheets. The best culture beats process every time, especially when it includes good music and a shared belief that you're all in it together.

## @ 4: Green in the Desert

Dubai, 2015. A layover turned into a legend. Kent and I had just wrapped up a client meeting in Bangkok, and our next stop was Dubai for partner discussions. As fate would have it, our trip landed on March 17th. St. Patrick’s Day.

Now, Dubai doesn't exactly scream "Irish party." But that’s the magic of the city; it's a place of paradoxes. Kent had heard about The Irish Village, a beloved expat haunt. "They've got Guinness on tap and full-on step dancers," he said with a grin. So we dropped our bags, found something vaguely green to wear, and hopped in a cab. The scene was unbelievable: flags waving, faces painted, crowds swaying to live fiddlers in the warm desert air.

It was a proper Irish celebration, respectfully and joyfully held in the heart of a Muslim-majority country. We met telco execs from Etisalat, engineers from London, and an Irish fiddler who flew in every year just for this night. By the third pint, Kent and I were dancing; yes, actual dancing with a group of South Africans and Koreans doing their best Riverdance impressions. It was unhinged and beautiful.

Amid the revelry, something clicked. This party was a metaphor for our careers. We were telecom wanderers, making unlikely connections happen between cultures and technologies that didn't speak the same language until we forced them to. Standing there, holding a cold pint of Guinness, I realized connection is about intent. It’s about showing up, being present, and choosing joy.

We didn’t talk about work once that night, but I’ve never felt more energized to get back to it the next day. Leadership isn't just about deadlines; it's about creating space for serendipity, for play, and for culture.

## @ 5: The Endless Boardroom

**Taipei, Taiwan (Circa 2014)**

You could smell the intensity before the meeting even started. We had a full-day technical workshop with Chunghwa Telecom (CHT), Taiwan’s behemoth operator, known for its unrelenting attention to detail. Kent and I walked in with laptops, hope, and the quiet optimism that comes from surviving worse. Nothing could have prepared us for the next nine hours.

The boardroom was enormous and acoustically dead, dominated by a long table that looked like it had hosted interrogations. It was immediately clear this wasn't a "tea and biscuits" demo. CHT had assembled a small army: architects, security experts, and procurement watchdogs. We were grilled. Properly.

Slide by slide. Protocol by protocol. One exec even asked us to explain Wi-Fi Roaming architecture from scratch after the coffee break. Kent, ever the rock, handled the technical questions with his classic poker face. I played backup, providing the commercial rationale and the business logic. Around hour six, even the secretary was sweating. When we finally wrapped, it felt less like a win and more like surviving a chess match with a grandmaster.

But then, night fell. We found ourselves in the Xinyi district, in front of a neon-lit Go-Go bar. Inside, it was loud, dark, chaotic, and exactly what we needed. We grabbed Taiwan Beers and finally laughed. "Bro," I said, "if this project goes live, I want it on my gravestone." Kent clinked his glass. "Only if the bartender knows the Diameter flow."

The best wins often come wrapped in exhaustion. Technical excellence and delivery charisma are a deadly duo. And sometimes, your most memorable boardroom reflections happen under neon lights with a cold beer. CHT didn't greenlight our proposal in the end, but that day was still a victory. Because in this business, surviving the grind with people you trust? That’s half the game.

## @ 6: When the Bartender Knows Your Order

**Hong Kong (Multiple Tours from 2012–2016)**

If Accuris had an unofficial second HQ in Asia, it was Hong Kong. The city was a magnet for roaming business, a playground for dealmakers. For me and Kent, it became a recurring stop, part deployment site, part therapy lounge. We knew the pubs, Delaney’s, Joe Bananas, Murphy’s and the bartenders knew us. Not in a "welcome back, sir" way, but in a "pint of Kilkenny and a Jameson neat?" kind of way.

One night stands out. We had just wrapped a week of demos and tender clarifications for China Mobile. It was one of those weeks where everything that could go wrong flirted with doing so. A buggy integration. An unresponsive server. A slide deck that refused to render fonts correctly. We fixed it all, with Kent hammering out code at 1 a.m. in his hotel room while I fielded client WhatsApps.

That Friday, we landed at Delaney’s. It started with Guinness and escalated to a round of shots we never ordered (thanks to our bartender friend). A live band was playing, and before we knew it, we were singing "Whiskey in the Jar" with a group of Korean businessmen and a Canadian software reseller. It was the kind of night that blurred into legend. Kent turned to me and said, "Bro, if AccuROAM crashes next week, we’re rebooting from here." We laughed like schoolkids.

These nights were pressure valves. The bar was where we processed the madness. Your crew matters more than your credentials. A drink shared after a chaotic week builds more trust than a well-written report. Burnout is real, but so is release. You have to find your version of Delaney’s.

## @ 7: Mission Islamabad

**Islamabad & Lahore, Pakistan (2013–2015)**

When the assignment for Pakistan came in, nobody wanted it. Security concerns, visa nightmares, political tensions, all the usual warnings were thrown at it. But Kent and I looked at each other and said, "Let's go." Why? Because when everyone else says no, that’s where the best stories are.

The visa process alone was an adventure, a week of back-and-forth with the embassy in Kuala Lumpur. Flying into Islamabad felt like stepping into a movie. Then came the checkpoints. Armed soldiers, full-body scans, and more questions than a job interview. At one point, we were stopped by soldiers with fully loaded automatic weapons because our cab driver missed a turn. Kent stayed calm. I… was less calm. But we made it.

We were there to support a Wi-Fi roaming integration pitch. It was a job nobody wanted, with legacy systems and no proper documentation. And yet, day by day, debug by debug, we got it moving. Kent was a magician, pulling out logs like a forensics expert. I played interpreter, trainer, and diplomat, winning trust and explaining the magic of roaming hubs to a room full of skeptics.

Midway through the trip, our partner asked if we’d do a quick day trip to Lahore, 400km away, to meet a prospect. Our response? "Why not." We jumped in a car, pitched Wateen Telecom for an hour, nailed it, and drove all the way back that same night. That 800km round trip was one of the most insane travel decisions we ever made, but also one of the most satisfying.

This trip was a masterclass in courage. It was proof that relationships matter more than PowerPoints. Kent and I didn't just walk into Pakistan; we showed up when no one else would. Today, when someone asks me about the toughest place I’ve worked, I smile and say: Islamabad. And I’d go again in a heartbeat.

## @ 8: 72 Hours in Sri Lanka

**Colombo, Sri Lanka (2012)**

It was a Thursday afternoon when the call came. "Khaw, can you fly to Colombo tomorrow? We’ve got a shot at a PCRF opportunity with SLT." No warning. No prep. Just the kind of last-minute scramble that defines business in APAC. I asked myself: *Sri Lanka, 72 hours, in and out. You in?* My gut replied: *Let’s crush it.*

The heat hits you first in Colombo, like walking into a sauna with palm trees. I checked into the Hilton, a rare slice of luxury in what would be a whirlwind trip. The view was stunning. The schedule was brutal. Within an hour, I was in a meeting room with our local partner, going through every tech angle and political minefield. The Sales VP, Amelia, and I wanted this deal. Badly.

The next day’s pitch was textbook intense. The SLT team was sharp and tough. I handled the product deep-dive, walking them through dynamic policy enforcement and QoS prioritization. Amelia worked the room, reading the non-verbal cues and aligning our proposal with their roadmap. It clicked. We weren't the biggest name in the room, but we had the most clarity. That’s what got us to the second round.

Back at the Hilton that evening, I looked out at the peaceful Indian Ocean. It was completely wasted on us. Our laptops were open, slide decks were flying. We had to land this, or we'd miss the window. We didn’t party. We didn’t swim. We just executed.

That trip taught me that speed and clarity win deals. The view means more when the work is done. And partners matter; we couldn't have done it without local insight. I flew back with bags under my eyes and a quiet confidence that we had nailed it. This business isn't just about networks and nodes. It's about moments where grit meets opportunity, and 72 hours can shape the next year.

## @ 9: Frozen in Waterloo

**Waterloo, Canada (2016–2017)**

Some business trips make you feel important. Others just make you feel cold. Waterloo, the home of Sandvine HQ, was both. The first time I flew in, it was -5°C, with snow piled like frozen dunes. “Welcome to Canada,” someone joked. “This is summer for us.”

Coming from the sweaty energy of Kuala Lumpur, the stillness of Waterloo was surreal. But inside Sandvine HQ, it was all action. Engineering brilliance, strategic depth, and a culture of openness that surprised me. I was there representing APAC customer success and sales engineering. The days were packed with planning cycles and strategy summits. The evenings? Full of beer, debates, and snow-covered pub crawls.

I never got used to the cold, but I learned to survive. Always know where the nearest Tim Hortons is. Don’t trust a sunny sky; that’s when it’s really freezing. And there was the visa hack: with a Canadian visa, you could sneak into the U.S. with less hassle. I became a pro at routing trips through Buffalo to attend meetings or just grab a greasy American burger.

On one trip, we drove out to Niagara Falls. I stood at the edge of that roaring curtain of water, mist freezing on my jacket, and felt something hit me. This job, this life, had brought me here. From debugging in KL to whiteboarding with VPs in Ontario, I had crossed not just time zones, but mental zones. I wasn't just chasing deals anymore; I was helping shape regional priorities.

Waterloo taught me that stillness is a form of strength. It taught me that global companies win when they listen to the people on the ground. And it taught me that cold builds clarity. You think deeper. And when your thoughts finally sharpen, they cut. I always came back from Waterloo with more than jet lag. I came back recalibrated.

## @ 10: From Sales Decks to Spotlights

**Hong Kong & Macau (2018)**

Every tech company has its annual Sales Kick-Off. But when you mix Hong Kong’s buzz with a bit of Ruckus flair, you don't just get a meeting. You get a spectacle.

It started like any other corporate event: ballroom, branding, a parade of PowerPoints. But this one had a pulse. We gathered at Hong Kong’s Harbourfront, overlooking the iconic skyline. I remember stepping onto the stage to talk about APAC strategy, clicker in hand, speaking to an audience from five continents. The energy was high, but so was the pressure. We were chasing aggressive targets. My team’s success was a linchpin for the entire region.

But after hours of charts and QBRs, the room needed oxygen. We found it across the water.

Once the final slide clicked off, the real kick-off began. A few of us boarded a high-speed ferry to Macau, the Vegas of the East. Bright lights, Bellagio vibes, and a night that danced between celebration and chaos.

What happened in Macau was legendary. The casino floor pulsed with telco execs pretending to be poker pros. A colleague won big on a slot machine, only to lose his badge (we found it later, somehow on a ceiling fan :-)). I ended up at a karaoke bar belting out Michael Learns to Rock, because of course "Paint My Love" is the anthem of underdog Wi-Fi deals. And yes, there was a pole dancing show. We didn’t plan it. We didn’t stop it. We just laughed. Because somewhere between the champagne and vendor gossip, we remembered that before we were professionals, we were people. People with stories, with pressure, who just for one night, needed to be more than their job titles.

Morale isn't built in meetings; it's built in shared stories and wild nights. Teams bond over being human together. I woke up the next morning blurry-eyed, with my phone at 2%. But in my inbox was a note from the Head of Sales: "Brilliant session. Can we discuss extending your team's charter?"

And that’s the thing. You can't always plan the win. But if you show up with heart, guts, and a little bit of madness, the universe sometimes gives you a shot.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Reframe the "wasted" time in your career. A flight delay isn’t a nuisance; it’s a forced window for reflection. A difficult business trip isn’t just a project; it’s a masterclass in resilience. The next time you travel with your team, intentionally schedule unstructured time, be it a team dinner or a walk around the city. The bonds forged and lessons learned when you are simply being human together are more valuable and enduring than anything you’ll accomplish in the boardroom.*

title: Consultant With a Cause
summary: Sometimes you pause your career not because you're tired, but because you need to reset the direction. In late 2018, I joined Fortesys Sdn Bhd, not as an engineer or a salesman, but as a Business Consultant.
content:
## Rebooting Vision at Fortesys (2018–2019)

Sometimes you pause your career not because you're tired, but because you need to reset the direction. In late 2018, I joined Fortesys Sdn Bhd, not as an engineer or a salesman, but as a Business Consultant. The brief was simple on paper: help reboot the company’s growth strategy across ASEAN. The reality? I walked into an organization with a ton of ambition but no map. So, I rolled up my sleeves and started asking the annoying questions.

## The Strategy Detox

The first thing we did was stop everything. Literally. We paused the pipeline reviews, shelved stale partnerships, and froze the quarterly fire drills. It was time to zoom out and ask the fundamental questions: "What do we actually sell?" "To whom?" "And why the heck should they care?" The answers, it turned out, were buried under layers of legacy assumptions and old PowerPoints. We stripped the messaging down to something human, something that would actually resonate in a boardroom. You can't scale what you don't understand. And you can't sell what doesn't work.

## Reconnecting with the Ground

We weren't Google, and we didn't need to pretend we were. What we had was our proximity to the field. We knew the resellers by name. We ate lunch with our local partners. That was our edge. So I pushed us back to the streets, visiting channel partners in Indonesia and reconnecting with grassroots integrators to learn what kept them up at night. Hint: It wasn't always the tech. It was logistics, margins, and the simple desire to be heard. Consulting isn't about frameworks. It's about witnessing.

## Small Wins, Big Ripples

We didn't land any ten-million-dollar contracts in those months. But we did reposition Fortesys as a thoughtful regional player, not just another box-mover. We created a scalable go-to-market model for emerging markets and laid the groundwork for future ICT services in Indonesia and beyond. Most importantly, we brought clarity. Sometimes the win isn't loud. It's quiet, strategic, and permanent.

## The Consultant’s Curse

There’s a moment in every consulting gig when you realize your main job is to make yourself obsolete. When that moment came, I knew I was done. The vision was clearer, the roadmap was drafted, and the local teams were ready to run. It was time for me to step aside and move toward the next chapter. That’s when M1 Singapore entered the frame.

I had scribbled on a whiteboard on my last day at Fortesys: "Every company is a signal. Some are loud but static. Others are soft but meaningful. My job was never to shout. It was to help you tune." That year was short but powerful. It taught me that not every career milestone needs a title upgrade. Sometimes, it’s about realignment.

And just as I was syncing back into that rhythm, destiny called from across the causeway. "You've advised. You've listened. Now build again. But bigger."

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *If your team or project feels stuck, perform a "Strategy Detox." Pause all non-essential activities for one week and force a return to the three simplest questions: 1. What do we actually sell? 2. To whom? 3. Why would they care?*
>
> *Get the answers not from internal documents but from your frontline partners and customers. Your goal as a leader is to provide a clear map and the right tools, then empower your team to navigate the journey on their own.*

title: MVNO, Maxx, and Me
summary: December 2019. I walked into M1 Singapore, straight into the Digital Office, a battalion formed for one purpose: transformation.
content:
## A tale of platforms and one very persistent product owner. (2019–2023)

December 2019. I walked into M1 Singapore, straight into the Digital Office, a battalion formed for one purpose: transformation. They didn’t want babysitters for legacy systems; they wanted revolutionaries. And I was tired of theory. I wanted to build again. They handed me the MVNE/MVNO portfolio. I grinned. This was the good stuff. No more slide decks. Just architecture, ambition, and a blank canvas.

## The MVNE Master Plan

Most people see Mobile Virtual Network Enabler (MVNE) platforms as boring plumbing. I saw them as empowerment technology, a way to spin up new telco brands overnight. So I started designing a multi-tenant digital platform that could host multiple MVNOs independently, scale regionally without technical migraines, and launch sub-brands like firecrackers. I called it my platform-of-platforms.

## The Launch List

In just 18 months, we launched and scaled MyRepublic, Gorilla Mobile, Geenet, Changi Mobile, and the head-turning M1 sub-brand, Maxx. We created flexible onboarding flows that made traditional telcos look ancient. We tied together payment gateways, digital identity, and lifestyle bundles for the ethnic market. All while balancing platform stability and C-suite ping pong. It was glorious chaos. Sometimes your job isn't to pick a lane. It's to build the highway.

## Maxx: The Side Project That Took Over

Oh, Maxx! It was the lovechild of simplicity and swagger. We built it like a startup inside a legacy company, lean team, fast pivots, and a sharp focus on SIM-only plans with a digital-first mindset. We gamified top-ups and polished the self-care app until it gleamed. We listened to what the community actually wanted. And it resonated. Maxx wasn't just another brand; it was a philosophy: honest plans, digital freedom, and no B.S. contracts.

## Behind the Scenes: Sleepless Success

Let’s not pretend it was all clean API calls and victory laps. We had midnight war rooms when provisioning queues jammed. We had tense meetings with partners over SLAs. We had developers fueled by caffeine and business teams running on pure adrenaline. But we kept moving. Progress doesn't always look pretty. Sometimes it looks like back-to-back incident tickets at 2 a.m. What made it work? Trust. We weren't just building for the market; we were building for each other.

## The Prepaid Transformation

Just when I thought things might stabilize, I got another tap on the shoulder: "Khaw, we need you to lead the prepaid transformation." Challenge accepted. This wasn't just about launching new plans; it was about reimagining the entire prepaid experience. I pushed for self-onboarding with digital KYC, seamless migration journeys, and a user experience that didn't feel like it was from 2003. Slowly, we turned prepaid from an afterthought into a strategic growth engine.

## A New Philosophy

Somewhere along the way, I jotted this on a whiteboard: "The best product managers don’t just manage features. They manage faith in the team, in the vision, and in the user." That became my compass. Every time someone said something was "impossible," I’d ask, "What’s really blocking us?" Nine times out of ten, it wasn't the technology. It was the mindset.

And let’s not forget, all of this was happening during the pandemic. Remote everything. Virtual launches. Teams working from home with toddlers on their laps and Wi-Fi that hated Zoom. And yet, we launched. We scaled. We thrived. Innovation isn't about big ideas. It's about resilience in motion.

## Preparing for Lift-Off

By late 2023, the platforms were built and the brands were launched. We’d shown what a digital telco could look like. And now, the mission was expanding. From sub-brands and MVNOs to a full, core BSS transformation. Next stop: Head of Platform for M1. This era taught me how to manage momentum, how to defend the customer’s voice, and how to refuse to settle for "good enough."

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Define your platform philosophy. Are you building a product with a finite set of features, or are you building a highway that empowers others to create their own vehicles? A leader’s most critical job during a transformation is to manage momentum and faith. When you face technical roadblocks, look for the underlying mindset that needs to shift. Championing this change and protecting your team from the ensuing chaos is how you turn a digital project into a digital movement.*

title: Platforms and Power Plays
summary: There’s a point in every journey where you stop climbing and start building the mountains themselves. For me, that was January 2024.
content:
## Leading the Digital Core at M1 (2024–2025)

There’s a point in every journey where you stop climbing and start building the mountains themselves. For me, that was January 2024. I became Head of Platforms, and then Head of Product Management a year later, at M1. I was handed the keys to the company’s digital brain: CRM, billing, charging systems, APIs, web, and mobile. All of it. The digital core. It wasn't a handover; it was a battlefield commission. Because the role came with an insane challenge: migrate two major businesses in one year, without breaking a single thing.

## The Migrations That Mattered

Let’s be clear: telco migrations are terrifying. They're high-risk, multi-year projects where every wrong move can mean customers can't top up their data or businesses lose trust. Now imagine doing it twice in a year. That was the brief. We had to move legacy platforms to new digital stacks, ensure zero downtime, and keep revenue flowing, all while users remained blissfully unaware.

And we did it. On time. Under insane pressure. Product leadership isn't just about delivery. It's about holding the line when everything is shaking.

## The Philosophy of Scale

I stopped thinking about features and started thinking about ecosystems. If the CRM doesn't sync with billing, customers get confused. If the charging system chokes, prepaid users lose faith. If the APIs break, our retail partners walk away. So I baked platform thinking into our team's DNA. In every sprint and every stand-up, we zoomed out before we dove in. We weren't just building products; we were building the foundations for the next decade.

## My Tenets for the Team

To survive the chaos, I came up with three simple rules:

1.  **Own the outcome.** Not the ticket. Not the slide deck. The real-world impact.

2.  **Simplify fiercely.** Complexity isn't a badge of honor. Simplicity is what scales.

3.  **Communicate like a human.** If your update can’t be understood by both a marketer and a sysadmin, rewrite it. These weren’t just rules; they were our survival guide.

## When the Dust Settled

After the migrations, something strange happened. The war rooms went quiet. The backlog cleared. And for the first time in months, I saw the team take a full, deep breath. That’s when I knew we hadn’t just survived. We had matured. Pressure doesn't break great teams. It reveals them.

## The Real Work Begins

With the firefighting over, we turned to creating real value. We enabled new SIM-only and device plan orchestrations. We accelerated platform readiness for the business. We scaled our API monetization and partner onboarding. I started pitching the digital core not as a cost center, but as the company's primary growth engine. And I made sure the C-suite saw it that way, too.

## Coaching the Next Generation

You know what else changed? Me. I stopped trying to be the smartest person in the room. Instead, I started coaching. I taught my team how to ask better questions and how to prioritize when everything feels urgent. I showed them how to manage up, sideways, and across time zones. This wasn't about me winning anymore. It was about making the entire team unstoppable. Your legacy isn't what you ship. It's who you uplift.

## The View from Here

So where does that leave me? Still running. Still building. Still asking tough questions in boardrooms and silly ones in stand-ups. And still believing, with the same certainty I had back in 2001 with that dial-up modem, that technology, when it's done right, doesn't just work. It empowers. It frees. And in the best cases, it just disappears.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *As a senior leader, your primary role must shift from being the best problem-solver to building the best problem-solvers. Codify your core leadership principles into simple, memorable rules (e.g., "Own the outcome, not the ticket"). Use these principles to coach your team daily. Measure your success not by the problems you solve, but by the number of problems that no longer need you to be in the room. Your legacy is not the platform you ship; it’s the leaders you create.*
