## The Brightest Team in the Telco Sky

After the dust settled from our second major platform migration across Prepaid, Maxx, MVNOs, CRM, Billing, and everything in between, I knew one thing for sure. You don't survive that kind of back-to-back transformation without an all-star team. And I was lucky. No, blessed. I had the kind of team people write books about: a crew made of brains, grit, banter, and a shared love for getting things done right. This chapter is for them. My band of signal warriors. My protocol poets. My midnight miracle-makers.

## Wai Kun – The Foundation 

If our systems had a heartbeat, Wai Kun would be the pulse. He doesn't chase the spotlight, but he holds everything together with a quiet force that anchors the entire team. When legacy chaos threatens to derail us, Wai Kun doesn't flinch. He clarifies, streamlines, and executes with surgical precision. He doesn't just know the Maxx and Prepaid systems; he thinks in them. He can untangle years of technical complexity in a matter of days. There are people who react to fires, and then there are people who prevent them from ever starting. That’s Wai Kun. Every high-performing team has a solid core. We’re lucky ours is named Wai Kun.

## Teddy – The Heartbeat of Recovery

When everything's on fire, we all say the same thing: "Get Teddy." He’s more than a fixer; he’s our first responder, our systems therapist. He dives into incidents headfirst; cool-headed, fast-fingered, and always ten steps ahead. But what makes him truly special is the compassion he brings to a crisis. He listens before he leaps, calming vendors and reassuring teams. When he shows up, the tension in the room drops, and the trust level skyrockets. He doesn't just fix the issue; he fixes the fear around it. Teddy is the soul of our support.

## Sandy – The Spark 

Sandy might be the youngest among us, but don’t let that fool you; she’s already operating at warp speed. With every challenge, she rises higher, attacking bugs and process puzzles with energy and razor-sharp intuition. She doesn't just learn; she absorbs, sharpens, and turns knowledge into value by the next sprint. She’s not waiting to be told what to do. She’s already doing it. And she’s inspiring the rest of us. Sandy doesn't just have potential; she’s making it real, right now.

## Sumit – The Strategist 

Sumit doesn't need to raise his voice to make waves. He listens, he connects the dots, and then, quietly, he changes the game. He’s the bridge between business and technology, between marketing logic and customer truth. He stepped into Prepaid Marketing and instantly elevated how we think about customer engagement. He’s the calm in the commercial chaos, the interpreter when silos get in the way. His strength is his ability to humanize strategy. Some people move meetings. Sumit moves momentum. He doesn't just represent alignment; he creates it.

## Reshir – The Clarity-Maker 

Reshir joined us quietly, but her mind stood out immediately. While others were still trying to grasp the chaos, she was already connecting the dots and asking the questions no one else thought to ask. She came in with focus, humility, and a hunger to learn. And she learned fast, growing from a sharp analyst into a commanding product leader. Today, she leads our MVNO product team, not because she chased a title, but because her results demanded it. She brings structure to complexity and clarity to confusion. Some leaders lead with loud energy. Reshir leads with quiet precision, and her clarity echoes louder than most.

## Goh Yi Ying – The North Star of Maxx 

Yi Ying was more than a steady hand; she was the unwavering compass that guided the Maxx product through all its complexity and change. With a deep mastery of the platform and a calm authority that never wavered, she anchored us through shifting priorities and impossible timelines. Her legacy isn’t just in the systems she helped build, but in the standard of excellence she left behind. Her leadership wasn't loud; it was respected. Her work always spoke for itself: consistent delivery and razor-sharp clarity.

When the waves got rough, we looked to Yi Ying; not because she shouted the loudest, but because she always knew the way. Though her path has taken a new direction, the clarity she brought continues to guide us. She wasn't just a part of the Maxx story; she helped write its most critical chapters. We miss her guidance immensely but are all cheering for her next big win.

## Alvin Siow – The Reluctant Maestro

Alvin didn’t start on my team. But somewhere along the journey, I asked him to lend a hand on a transformation project. That one hand quickly became two. He stepped in quietly, learned fast, and before long was orchestrating some of our most critical deliveries with the finesse of a seasoned maestro. From migrations to launches, Alvin grew into the role, and eventually into my team, by proving himself over and over. Today, he’s the glue that holds our timelines together. Alvin isn't just dependable; he's quietly indispensable. And along the way, he became a father. Balancing late-night calls with diaper duty? That’s legendary.

## Wee Seng – The Grand Master

And then there's Wee Seng. Part strategist, part tactician, part philosopher, "The Grand Master" lives up to the name. He's not just respected; he's revered. Wee Seng doesn't just move the pieces on the board; he sees ten steps ahead. He can look at a telco diagram and instantly spot the weak link. He's led digital transformations, grown PMO into a force, and mentored us all with a humility that only comes from true mastery. Oh, and he’s faster than most of us at both running and system rollouts. The man is a machine.

## The Constellation That Shines Together 

What makes this team magic isn't just the individual talent; it's the trust. It's the way everyone shows up for each other. The way we cover gaps, celebrate wins, and argue over user flows simply because we care. We've navigated org changes, tight budgets, and surprise executive escalations, and through it all, this team never faltered. They only got sharper. You don't build great platforms with tools. You build them with people like this.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Take 30 minutes and write your own "All-Star Constellation" list. For every member of your direct team, identify their unique superpower in one sentence. What do they do better than anyone else? When do they truly shine? Use this insight in your next one-on-one to tell them specifically what you value about them. You will not only foster loyalty, but you will also begin to see your team as a strategic collection of talents that you can deploy with greater precision and impact.*

title: Home Ground, Heavy Static
summary: There is a particular kind of irony in coming home to do the hardest migration of your career.
content:
There is a particular kind of irony in coming home to do the hardest migration of your career.

In January 2026, after six years of building digital platforms and battling through back-to-back cutovers in Singapore, I packed up my life and returned to Kuala Lumpur. The plan was straightforward on paper: step into Maxis as Program Director for IT Transformation, take ownership of a full-stack BSS overhaul, and steer the ship from legacy architecture onto a modern stack.

On paper, it looked like a natural next chapter. In reality, it felt like walking into a live server room where the racks were already humming at redline, the blueprints were still being debated, and half the stakeholders had different ideas of where the doors were supposed to be.

If Part 1 of my career was learning how to read a single signal, and Singapore was learning how to build platforms from scratch, Maxis became the ultimate stress test in signal-to-noise ratio.

## The Anatomy of a Full-Stack Beast

Anyone who has worked inside a tier-one telco knows that replacing a Business Support System isn't a software upgrade—it’s open-heart surgery while the patient is running a half-marathon.

The scope wasn't a neat, isolated greenfield sandbox. It was the entire nervous system of the business: CRM, Product Catalog, Billing and Charging, and the dense web of integration layers holding everything together. On one side sat the core platform vendor, carrying their own playbooks, timelines, and delivery rhythms. On the other sat an ecosystem of more than a hundred surrounding third-party systems—legacy touchpoints, downstream dependencies, payment gateways, partner interfaces, and custom workarounds built over decades.

When you have over a hundred external systems wired into a core transformation, every single interface is a potential single point of failure. A minor schema change in one corner triggers a silent timeout three hops away. A delayed sign-off in one business unit freezes an end-to-end test cycle across five squads. You don’t just manage a project plan at that scale; you manage a living, breathing spiderweb where pulling one thread vibrates the entire room.

## When the Static Isn’t in the Code

In my earlier years, I used to think the hardest problems lived inside log files, protocol traces, and architecture diagrams. Give me a broken link or a failing charging flow, and I knew how to isolate the fault, trace the packet, and fix it.

By 2026, I knew better. The heaviest static rarely comes from the servers. It comes from people.

Stepping into an entrenched transformation meant inheriting more than technical debt—it meant stepping into a less-than-ideal working environment shaped by competing agendas, territorial habits, and stakeholders who viewed change as a threat rather than a lifeline. Alignment wasn't given; it had to be wrestled out of every meeting.

Then there was the friction from above. Navigating difficult managers while trying to shield a delivery team from organizational whiplash is an art form nobody teaches in engineering school. When leadership styles clash—when escalation becomes a reflex instead of a tool, or when optics matter more than actual architectural readiness—you quickly realize that your real job isn't just technical governance. It’s acting as a human voltage regulator. You absorb the spikes from the top so the engineers and leads on the ground have enough clean power to actually build.

There were days when the environment tested every ounce of patience I had accumulated over twenty-five years. Days when stakeholder politics consumed more bandwidth than system integration. Days when the easiest thing in the world would have been to step back, point at the org chart, and let the friction win.

## Breakfast War Rooms and Lunchtime Kopi

When the official calendar is packed with rigid governance calls and uphill stakeholder battles, you learn quickly that the real work rarely happens inside the formal meeting invite. It happens around food.

Most mornings, before the office even officially wakes up and the inbox starts screaming, the working team and I gather for breakfast. No slide decks, no formal minutes, no posturing—just half-boiled eggs, toast, and candid conversation. Over that quiet hour before the daily storm hits, we catch up as human beings first, then untangle the messiest blockers on the board. Problems that would take three escalation emails and a two-hour committee call to dissect get sorted out in fifteen minutes between bites. It sets our compass before we even badge into the building.

And by midday, after surviving the morning's regular meeting cadence—the status interrogations, the shifting goalposts, the relentless pressure—lunchtime *kopi* becomes our pressure-release valve. Sitting together away from the screens, venting over coffee and trading dry jokes about the absurdity of corporate life, the tension finally drops. Laughter in the middle of a grueling transformation isn't a distraction; it’s oxygen. Those shared breaks remind us we aren't just cogs grinding through a migration plan—we're a crew watching each other's backs, and that camaraderie is what keeps everyone showing up tomorrow.

## Ploughing Through for the Long Game

We didn't back down.

When the environment isn't ideal and the management terrain is rough, you fall back on what has always worked in the trenches: clarity, cadence, and stubborn persistence.

You stop waiting for perfect organizational harmony—because in a transformation of this size, it never arrives—and start focusing ruthlessly on the target outcome. You break the hundred-system monster down into concrete, non-negotiable milestones. You translate vague stakeholder anxieties into clear technical dependencies. You protect your morning rituals, guard your team's morale over *kopi*, and keep pushing forward, one resolved blocker at a time.

It isn't glamorous work. There are no celebratory launch photos yet—this chapter is still being written in real time, in breakfast stalls, integration war rooms, and late-evening syncs across Kuala Lumpur.

But that is the real test of the builder's mindset. Anyone can lead when the wind is at their back, the team is hand-picked, and the mandate is crystal clear. You find out what your twenty-five years of scar tissue are actually worth when the weather turns, the static gets loud, and you still keep the signal moving toward the finish line.

---

## Signal Debrief: Leading When the Static Gets Loud

- **The Situation:** Returning home to lead a full-stack BSS transformation across CRM, Product Catalog, Billing and Charging, a core platform vendor, and more than 100 third-party integrations inside a complex organizational environment.
- **The Noise:** Competing stakeholder agendas, territorial friction, difficult management dynamics, rigid status-meeting cadences, and the sheer technical sprawl of over a hundred interconnected systems.
- **The Signal:** In a large-scale transformation, formal governance rarely creates alignment—informal trust does. Shielding your builders from top-down turbulence and creating unscripted spaces (before the workday starts and over midday *kopi*) unlocks faster problem-solving and sustains morale far better than another escalation call.
- **How to Use This Signal:**
  - **Be the voltage regulator:** Absorb unreasonable executive pressure at your level instead of passing raw panic down to your engineering and delivery leads.
  - **Create zero-slide rituals:** Establish a casual, pre-meeting touchpoint with your core working team to clear real blockers before corporate theater begins.
  - **Protect the pressure valve:** Never underestimate shared breaks and humor during a multi-year grind—psychological safety and camaraderie are operational necessities, not perks.

title: The Long Game
summary: Twenty-five years. Countless late nights, product launches, platform crashes, and impossible deadlines.
content:
## Legacy in Motion (2025 and beyond)

Twenty-five years. Countless late nights, product launches, platform crashes, and impossible deadlines. And a million moments where I asked myself, *Is this it?* But every time I thought I'd hit a peak, the trail kept climbing.

From that windowless KL office in the early 2000s, dreaming beyond a dial-up screen, to leading full-stack telco transformations with all-star teams, this journey was never a straight line. It zigzagged. It looped. Sometimes it glitched. But it never stopped moving. The long game isn't a straight road. It’s a series of detours you learn to dance through.

## The Heavy Lifting

Let’s not romanticize it. I've missed flights. I've missed my kids' bedtimes. I've hit dead ends with a product launch and had to rebuild from scratch. I’ve stared at dashboards full of failing KPIs and faced rooms where I had to defend ideas no one else believed in. And still, I showed up. Because this game rewards those who stay long enough to learn the rules, break them when needed, and then teach others to do the same. I used to think success was about speed. Now I know it’s about stamina. Anyone can lead during launch week. The real ones lead during the rollback.

## Rewiring My Own Metrics

At some point, you stop counting promotions. You stop obsessing over your CV. And you start asking different questions: Did I move something that mattered? Did I create momentum where there was inertia? Did I leave the room better than I found it?

I measure my work by different signals now. The speed at which a junior teammate grows. A stressed vendor saying, "Thanks for being fair." The sound of the team laughing together on a tough day. Those are the metrics no dashboard will ever track, but they're the ones that last.

## What Legacy Really Means

Let’s be honest: platforms break. Tech stacks get sunsetted. Roadmaps pivot. But what endures? The culture you quietly protect. The people who found their voice because you made space for it. The next generation of leaders who are now running their own shows because you once believed in them. That’s the only legacy that matters. And if I’ve left even a few fingerprints in those spaces, then every long night was worth it.

## Still Running

Yes, I’ve done a lot. No, I’m not done. The world is moving faster, tech is morphing, and AI is writing code. But one truth remains: leadership is still human. And that’s where I come in. I’m not chasing the next big job. I’m chasing the next big impact. Maybe I’ll mentor startups. Maybe I’ll build something bold and wild again. Or maybe I’ll just keep telling stories like this one, to remind people that this business isn’t just about infrastructure; it’s about people, possibilities, and persistence. Whatever comes next, I'm showing up ready.

## Final Signal

If you’re reading this, wondering what comes after the grind, here’s my note to you: Don’t wait for clarity; build your way through the fog. Don’t over-polish your journey; your scars are your proof. And don’t forget that people will forget the Jira epic, but they’ll remember how you made them feel when things got tough.

I've lived through protocols and pivots, migrations and transformations. I've been the rookie, the rebel, the regional lead, the guy with the pitch, and the guy fixing the bug. I've been the one asked, "How did you get here?"

The answer is simple: "By playing the Long Game, with heart, with hustle, and with hope."

And trust me, I’m still playing.

> **💡 How to use this signal**
>
>
> *Conduct a personal "Legacy Audit" at the end of each quarter. Ask yourself three questions: 1. Did I move something that mattered? 2. Did I create momentum where there was none? 3. Did I leave the people in the room better than I found them?*
>
> *Let the answers, not your job title or the size of your budget, guide your next move. A great career isn't a sprint to a destination; it's a long game of building stamina, accumulating wisdom, and playing with heart.*

content:
Strava / Instagram - @botak.on.wheels

## From Strava Stats to Life Lessons (2020–2025)

If my professional story is about navigating networks, my athletic journey is the quiet heartbeat behind it all. For years, while sprinting through meetings, I was also lacing up for dawn runs and long weekend rides. And it’s this parallel journey, tracked obsessively on Strava, that has grounded me, shaped me, and transformed me.

It all started on two wheels. Cycling was my escape, a space to decompress after 14-hour days. Then, one day, something shifted. Wee Seng, our Grandmaster at work, dragged a few of us out for a run. What began as a friendly jog evolved into marathons, half-marathons, and eventually, my own rebirth as a runner.

By 2025, I found myself exploring even further: biathlons, swim challenges, and the brutal but addictive world of HYROX and other fitness games. From that first group ride to these multi-sport weekends, Strava has tracked years of sweat and satisfaction. But this chapter isn't just about sports. It’s about the human upgrade that came with it. From engineer to leader. From tired to tireless. From ordinary to something more.

## The Pedal That Started It All

It began with the bike. Cycling expanded my world, literally. I racked up over 32,000 kilometers across more than 750 rides, from city commutes to cross-border tours. It became my moving meditation. On long solo rides, ideas would unravel mid-climb and product strategies would form between turns. Hills became points of reflection; descents felt like clarity breaking through fog. Riding didn't just help me move; it helped me make sense of everything else.

The highlights were many: an AUDAX 200km ride in Singapore, the Tour de Bintan and Tour de Batam with Alister, Ivan, and Emad, the LeTape Desaru with the Lake Odyssey Riders, and multiple NTU Bike Rallies. But the most memorable ride? Our first team outing to Kukup. While most of the crew took vans, Wai Kun, Sumit, and I took the long way, on two wheels, across the Causeway and into the heart of rural Johor. It wasn't just the palm-lined roads; it was the freedom, the camaraderie, and the joy of journeying through sleepy fishing towns where time seemed to pause. We laughed, we raced, we stopped for juice at roadside stalls. That ride was symbolic of team, of grit, and of the quiet magic that happens when work friends become ride companions.

Cycling taught me about pacing, an essential leadership skill. You can't sprint up every hill. You learn to conserve, to push when needed, and to regroup after a setback.

## Becoming the Runner

It started with a single run. No coach, no plan. Just a need to shake off the stress of a long week. That run became a routine, and the routine became a lifestyle. Over the last few years, I’ve logged over 300 runs covering more than 2,000 kilometers. Every kilometer told a story of turning restlessness into rhythm.

Running became a form of meditation. Nothing reset my brain after an intense product launch like a dawn run with Teddy and Wai Kun. In 2024, I took on my first full marathon, the SCSM, alongside Wee Seng. I clocked 5 hours and 19 minutes. Not elite, but for someone who started late, it was a testament to pure grit. My half marathon PB is 2 hours and 5 minutes. And the real win? I wasn't just running races; I was running towards a better version of myself.

## Multisport Days: From Sentosa Sands to HYROX Arena

I’ve always believed growth happens in unfamiliar terrain. That’s what drew me to multisport, where the real challenge isn't just endurance but transition, variety, and recalibrating in motion. In 2025, I kicked off the year with the NUS Biathlon at Sentosa, a sunlit swim-and-run that tested my breath and my willpower. There was something raw about exiting the sea, heart racing, and pushing through the sand. I also revisited the Singapore T100 Duathlon in both 2024 and 2025, a blur of transitions that was a true test of mental gear-shifting. I even tackled the National Vertical Marathon, climbing toward a goal that was more than altitude.

But the standout experience? The 2025 HYROX Asia Championship, Corporate Relay. Four of us from work, Teddy, Reshir, Yi Ying, and I, signed up with barely two team sessions under our belts. It was a bold move. HYROX is a brutal mix of functional fitness and endurance racing: the ski-erg, the sled push, the farmer’s carry, sandbag lunges. Every station is designed to break you down and then build you back up. We went in undertrained, over-caffeinated, and fueled by adrenaline. And somehow, it clicked. We cheered each other on, swapped roles when someone faltered, and pushed past our limits together. I still remember the shared high at the finish line. No podium, just the feeling of "We did it. As a team." In many ways, HYROX was a condensed version of my career: messy, unpredictable, and entirely reliant on trust and teamwork.

These pursuits reminded me that transformation comes from choosing new arenas and showing up, even when you’re not ready. That mindset took me to my most recent challenge: the Redline Fitness Games in Kuala Lumpur. This was a pure, explosive test of power across 12 relentless stations. The goal was simple: go hard, transition fast, leave nothing in the tank. I pushed through the full-body burn of the Ski-Erg, endured gritty Deadball Burpees, and hauled kettlebells in the Farmer's Carry until my grip screamed. Station after station, from the Sandbag Gauntlet to the leg-shaking Sled Push & Pull, it was a battle against myself. I crushed all 12 stations in 46 minutes, a personal victory that felt less like a race and more like a statement: I’m still hungry, still pushing, and still finding my red line.

## Hiking Wisdom: Leading from Behind

And then there were the hikes, quieter, slower, and deeply grounding. The Monkey Canopy trail in Bandar Sungai Long taught me about perspective. Leadership, I realized, isn’t always about pace. Sometimes, it’s about choosing the right path and lifting others along the way. One morning in Kuala Lumpur’s Taman Tugu Negara brought it all home. My family and I wandered through the trails, unhurried and unplugged. No Strava stats, no summit selfies. Just shared stories, held hands, and muddy shoes. As my kids led the way, I followed, not correcting or rushing, just watching them explore. That day reminded me that while solo pursuits sharpen your edge, shared journeys nourish the soul.

## The Discipline Muscle

On average, I train for about six hours a week, with two runs and two rides. But those hours aren't just logged; they're earned. Carved out between Zoom calls, around family time, and through sheer willpower when motivation is low. The goal was never perfection; it was persistence. And over time, this routine became a sanctuary. It's the quiet engine that keeps my leadership sharp and my stress in check. The same determination that gets me through a tight deadline helps me finish a 140km ride on four hours of sleep. Fitness and career success are fueled by the same thing: consistency.

## The Numbers That Mattered

Strava never lied. It showed me my peaks and my plateaus. It became my personal performance review, without bias or politics. It was just raw truth in graphs and heart rate zones. It humbled me. And with every tracked ride and logged run, I learned to self-correct, to own my patterns, and to celebrate the effort, not just the outcome. The tool taught me how to lead myself long before I ever led others.

## Endurance and Leadership: The Hidden Link

Here’s the real truth: sports made me a better leader. They taught me to breathe through chaos, to celebrate the small wins, and to persist when fatigue blurs the finish line. I've managed complex platform migrations and handled 2 a.m. firefighting. The endurance I built on the saddle and on the running trail mirrored that mental stamina. I became more patient, more empathetic, less reactive. You don't survive telco transformations by brute force. You survive by pacing, fueling right, recovering well, and showing up again the next day. Just like in sport.

## What I’ve Learned

- **Progress is boring but powerful.** It happens in the early alarms and the unglamorous reps.

- **You are your own competition.** I stopped chasing others’ metrics and started defining my own.

- **You’re stronger than you think.** Always. Every long run reminded me I could go further.

- **Fun matters.** Some of my best friendships and ideas came to me on a saddle or a trail.

## Final Words

This chapter wasn't about medals. It was about movement. Movement that mirrored growth, that burned off ego, and that brought me closer to the leader I was meant to be. I may never podium, but I’m in the race. And I’m not stopping anytime soon. Strava may track the miles, but I measure my journey in mindset, heart, and purpose. So if you see me running before sunrise or pedaling past the city lights, know this: I’m still becoming. And I’m loving the ride.
